design_detail: Letter to the editor (Addiction 2011;106:1365-1368). Single author. The letter's text runs from p. 1365 to p. 1367 and its reference list ends at the top of p. 1368, where a separate letter by Fisk, Murphy, Montgomery and Wareing begins (that letter is not part of this card). It re-interprets Halpern et al. (2011), a cross-sectional study of people who used ecstasy with minimal exposure to other drugs, as consistent with serotonergic neurotoxicity. Evidence used: the letter's reading of Halpern et al.'s tables, a 2009 Health Technology Assessment meta-analysis (Rogers et al., 2009), the author's own earlier review (Parrott, 2006) and model, and a short list of imaging and electrophysiology studies. No methods, no search, no new data; 25 references. The letter has no sections; locators count its nine running-text paragraphs from the start of the letter (block quotations are not counted).
can_establish: What the author argues about Halpern et al. (2011), and which numbers from that study and from other papers he uses to argue it.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy causes the test differences the letter discusses: it adds no data, and its reading of the cited studies is the author's own.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letter). The study discussed is Halpern et al. (2011): people in Salt Lake City who used ecstasy and reported comparatively slight use of other drugs, against similar-aged occasional rave attendees who had never used ecstasy (p. 1365, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the author chooses which findings and studies to discuss.
sample.selection_effects: The letter discusses the Halpern et al. results that fit the author's model and cites mainly studies reporting deficits (refs 7-20), including several from the author's group. It does not mention that Halpern et al. attribute the lower vocabulary score of their ecstasy group to premorbid ability (checked by this reader in Halpern et al., 2011, PMC HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph).

exposure.measurement: As reported from Halpern et al. (2011): self-reported lifetime occasions of use; median 43.5 lifetime occasions; median 121 days since last use (pp. 1365-1366).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime occasions only, as reported: median 43.5; subgroups with fewer than 50 and with 50 or more lifetime occasions; 6 of the 22 people in the heavier subgroup had used on 150 or more occasions (p. 1366, 6th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: The letter stresses the light use of other drugs in the ecstasy group: median 10 lifetime alcohol intoxications, median 10 lifetime cannabis intoxications, median 0 cigarettes a day (interquartile range 0-0.3) (pp. 1365-1366, 4th paragraph). It does not give the control group's figures; in Halpern et al.'s Table 1 (checked by this reader, PMC HTML) alcohol intoxications were the same in both groups (median 10) and cannabis intoxications were higher in the ecstasy group (median 10 against 1).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Median 121 days since last ecstasy use, as reported (p. 1366, 8th paragraph, bracketed note).

comparison.controls: As reported: similar-aged occasional rave attendees who had never used ecstasy and had some slight use of other drugs (p. 1365, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The letter does not discuss pre-use differences between the groups. It counts the ecstasy group's lower vocabulary score among the impairments (p. 1366, 5th paragraph), although vocabulary is usually read as an index of premorbid ability, as Halpern et al. themselves read it.

outcomes.instruments: As listed from Halpern et al. (2011): Wechsler Memory Scale spatial span, WAIS digit-symbol, vocabulary and digits backwards, grooved pegboard, trail-making A and B, California verbal learning test, Revised Strategy Application Test (p. 1366). From Rogers et al. (2009): RAVLT immediate and delayed word recall, RBMT immediate and delayed prose recall, digit span forwards and backwards, and NART IQ (p. 1365, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Any test with a lower group mean at p<0.05 is called an impairment or deficit; no norms or clinical cut-offs are used.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: The letter rejects Halpern et al.'s reading of their uncorrected multiple comparisons as probable chance findings (p. 1366, 5th paragraph) but applies or proposes no correction itself.

analysis.effect_sizes: None given. The letter cites p values only: for Halpern et al.'s overall comparison, spatial span forwards P<0.04, digit-symbol P<0.02, vocabulary P<0.01, digits backwards P<0.05 and grooved pegboard with the non-dominant hand P<0.02 (p. 1366, 5th paragraph); the pegboard difference P=0.02 overall and P=0.003 for the heavier subgroup (p. 1366, 7th paragraph); from Rogers et al. (2009), pooled digit span P=0.017 against polydrug-using controls and pooled verbal immediate recall P<0.001 over 27 studies (p. 1365, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Lists the overall-group differences at p of 0.05 or below but not that most of Halpern et al.'s 15 tests did not differ, and treats the vocabulary difference as a drug effect. It reports that the two subgroups did not generally differ and that the moderate subgroup was sometimes more impaired (p. 1366, 6th paragraph), without saying that this pattern runs against a dose-related effect on those tests.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The letter's own numbers describe a study in which a few of many tests were lower in the ecstasy group at p values between 0.01 and 0.05 without correction for multiple comparisons, in which the lighter and heavier subgroups mostly did not differ, and in which one of the lower scores (vocabulary) is a measure usually taken to reflect ability before drug use. Two tests (strategy application and the non-dominant-hand pegboard) were lower in the heavier subgroup.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The letter concludes that Halpern et al. have shown MDMA to be cognitively damaging even under conditions the author calls neuroprotective, and that the study confirms rather than refutes neurotoxicity (p. 1367, 9th paragraph). It treats the light other-drug use of the sample as the reason the deficits were modest. Causal language is drawn from an uncorrected cross-sectional comparison; the alternative readings that Halpern et al. give (premorbid differences, chance) are named only to be rejected.

timeline.event: Pilot study of people who used ecstasy with minimal other drug use, with deficits only in the heavier-use subgroup (Halpern et al., 2004, as described in this letter, p. 1366); critique by Lyvers and Hasking (2004), cited by Lyvers (2011).
Halpern et al. (2011): 52 people who used ecstasy and 59 non-using rave attendees; few differences on 15 tests.
Commentary reading the same study as strengthening the case against functionally significant neurotoxicity.
This letter, and on the same page a separate letter by Fisk, Murphy, Montgomery and Wareing criticizing the sample and the choice of tests (not carded).
The same author's narrative review describes Halpern et al. (2011) differently from this letter (see card sc_parrott_2013, reporting issues).

replication.where_it_stands: The letter is one side of a published disagreement over the same data set; the other side is the original authors' reading and Lyvers (2011). Neither side adds data. The disagreement turns on uncorrected p values and on whether pre-existing differences explain the few lower scores, which a cross-sectional design cannot settle.

funding.declared_conflicts: No declaration of interests is printed for this letter. The "Declarations of interest: None" on p. 1368 belongs to the following letter by Fisk et al.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Swansea University, UK. The argument is framed by the author's own earlier review (Parrott, 2006) and bio-energetic stress model, and the author is a co-author of two of the studies cited in support (Fox et al., 2002; Burgess et al., 2011). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the letter.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that tests people before and after they start using ecstasy, with minimal use of other drugs, measures premorbid ability (including vocabulary) at baseline, pre-registers a small set of primary tests with correction for multiple comparisons, and retests a non-using control group over the same interval.

domains.note: A letter: no search or selection criteria; studies are chosen to support the argument.
The cited studies reporting deficits are not appraised; Halpern et al.'s own explanations (premorbid ability, chance) are dismissed without analysis.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The interpretive frame is the author's own review and model; two supporting studies are co-authored by him.
A causal conclusion (cognitively damaging) is drawn from uncorrected cross-sectional differences, and the model is used as if it were evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a drug effect in the study discussed
domains.note: Under-represented: the many tests that did not differ, the lack of a consistent subgroup gradient, and the premorbid reading of the vocabulary difference.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a letter (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The letter is an advocacy re-reading of one study. It may be cited for the author's argument and for the numbers it quotes from Halpern et al. (2011), which this reader found to match that study's Table 2 for the five tests listed; it should not be cited as evidence that ecstasy caused the differences.

key_findings.finding: Thesis: the author argues that the modest deficits found by Halpern et al. (2011) are consistent with current knowledge of MDMA's adverse cognitive effects and neurotoxic properties, and concludes that the study confirms rather than refutes MDMA neurotoxicity, even with careful use.

As reported from the meta-analysis by Rogers et al. (2009): marked variation across studies; pooled digit span lower in people who used ecstasy than in polydrug-using controls (P=0.017); pooled verbal immediate recall composite lower over 27 studies (P<0.001); 6 of 7 meta-analysed variables (RAVLT immediate and delayed recall, RBMT immediate and delayed prose recall, digit span forwards and backwards) lower, and NART IQ not different.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the meta-analysis was not read; no effect sizes or intervals are given in the letter.

key_findings.finding: The author's earlier review named four factors behind variable findings (lifetime dose, intensity of use per session, environmental co-stimulation and other drugs) and reported that groups with fewer than about 50 lifetime occasions were generally not significantly impaired while groups above it often were; Halpern et al.'s median was 43.5 lifetime occasions.

Other drug use in Halpern et al.'s ecstasy group, as reported: median 10 lifetime alcohol intoxications, median 10 lifetime cannabis intoxications and median 0 cigarettes a day (interquartile range 0-0.3); the author describes the sample as relatively health-conscious and careful in its drug use.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph, continued at the top of p. 1366 (left column)

key_findings.finding: Five tests lower in the ecstasy group than in controls in Halpern et al.'s Table 2, as listed: Wechsler Memory Scale spatial span forwards P<0.04, WAIS digit-symbol P<0.02, WAIS vocabulary P<0.01, WAIS digits backwards P<0.05, grooved pegboard non-dominant hand P<0.02. The author rejects Halpern et al.'s reading that such differences are probably chance findings from uncorrected multiple comparisons. He notes that trail-making B and California verbal learning, tests he says are often impaired, did not differ.
key_findings.note: Checked by this reader against Halpern et al. (2011), PMC HTML, Table 2: the five tests and p values match (printed there as 0.04, 0.02, 0.01, 0.05 and 0.02). Raven's matrices, also at p=0.05 in that table, is not listed.

key_findings.finding: Subgroups: with moderate use defined as fewer than 50 and heavy use as 50 or more lifetime occasions, the two subgroups did not generally differ, and on some measures the moderate subgroup was more impaired; only 6 of the 22 people in the heavier subgroup had used on 150 or more occasions, and the subgroups' lifetime use was not reported. The Revised Strategy Application Test showed a dose-related impairment, which Halpern et al. read as poorer strategic self-regulation and perhaps greater reflection impulsivity.
key_findings.locator: 6th paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Grooved pegboard: no difference with the dominant hand; with the non-dominant hand the ecstasy group was slower than controls (P=0.02) and the heavier subgroup more so (P=0.003 against controls). Halpern et al. thought this probably chance; the author reads it as a deficit in higher cognitive control.

Imaging evidence cited for serotonergic deficits: a review concluding that lower serotonin transporter (SERT) density is the most robust finding (Cowan, 2007); a PET study of 49 people abstinent from ecstasy and 50 controls with SERT binding lower in every cortical region (-19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), associated with cumulative lifetime use and maximum use on one occasion, persisting after control for confounds including other drug use, and correlated with cognitive performance (Kish et al., 2010); SERT-cognition correlations (McCann et al., 2008); and one fMRI and one ERP study.
key_findings.locator: 8th paragraph (p. 1366, right column, continued on p. 1367)
key_findings.note: Second-hand descriptions of studies not read here.

key_findings.finding: Halpern et al.'s median time since last ecstasy use was 121 days, which the author takes to make the findings relevant to lasting toxicity.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the letter's quotations of Halpern et al. differ in wording from the source: the letter has the differences "report chance associations" introduced by "More probably", where Halpern et al. write "More likely" and "represent"; and it has the pegboard difference "due probably to chance", where the source says "likely due to chance" and attributes this to exploratory analyses (checked in Halpern et al., 2011, PMC HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the meaning is close, but the quotations should be re-checked against the source before reuse.

reporting_issues.issue: Vocabulary is counted among the drug-related impairments, but Halpern et al. report the lower vocabulary score as a group characteristic (Results, 2nd paragraph) and attribute it to premorbid ability (Discussion, 1st paragraph); the letter does not mention this.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the five differences offered as evidence of neurotoxicity is more plausibly a pre-existing difference; the case for neurotoxicity rests on four uncorrected p values.

reporting_issues.issue: P values are printed as inequalities (P<0.04 and so on) where the source gives exact values, and digits backwards at p=0.05 is called significant while Raven's matrices at the same p=0.05 is not listed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the threshold for calling a test impaired is applied inconsistently.

reporting_issues.issue: The same author's 2013 review describes Halpern et al. (2011) differently: it says the heavier subgroup was impaired on spatial span forwards and digit span backwards, whereas this letter (correctly, by Halpern et al.'s Tables 2 and 3) attributes these differences to the overall group and says the subgroups did not generally differ.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should cite Halpern et al.'s tables, not either description by this author; see card sc_parrott_2013.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1365-1368 (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2011_ReinterpretationOfHalpern.pdf), all pages read and pp. 1366-1368 rendered; the letter by Fisk et al. on p. 1368 read only to separate it from this letter. Quotations and numbers attributed to Halpern et al. (2011) were checked against that paper's PMC full text (PMC3053129) in this reader's own browser tab.
